title: Exclusive-Banks rush to swap higher-risk credit assets for Bank of England cash
description: , Lawrence White and David Milliken LONDON, Sept 2 (Reuters) - British banks are increasingly pledging higher-risk assets such as loans linked to high-interest store cards and vehicle
fullText:
LONDON, Sept 2 (Reuters) - British banks are increasingly pledging higher-risk assets such as loans linked to high-interest store cards and vehicle leases as collateral at the Bank of England, a Reuters review of BoE filings shows.

On August 18, banks pledged £1.9 billion ($2.6 billion) worth of the BoE's highest-risk type of collateral ‌at its weekly auction for six-month funds, its data shows, the most since March 2020 and three times as much as in the previous week.

In total, Reuters calculations show the BoE ‌has about £17.8 billion of what it calls "Level C" collateral on its books from its Indexed Long-Term Repo (ILTR), up from £8.7 billion a year ago and under £1 billion in mid-2024.

Such transactions show the extent to which Britain's central bank is exposed to higher-risk and ​potentially illiquid assets. The European Central Bank, meanwhile, has tightened its criteria for acceptable collateral in recent years, worried that a central bank stamp of approval increases demand for riskier securities that could be hard to sell in a crisis.

A BoE spokesperson said the ILTR was designed to allow firms to use a broad range of assets as collateral while allowing the BoE to protect itself through what it described as robust risk management.

"Our facilities are open for business and we welcome their increased use," the spokesperson said.

British commercial banks use cash held in accounts at the BoE for wholesale transactions. The growing use of the ILTR to receive this ‌cash is an intended consequence of the BoE's 2022 decision to reverse ⁠the £895 billion of quantitative easing it undertook from 2009 to 2021, which flooded the financial system with cash.

The securitisation of mortgage-backed debt and other loans was a major contributor to the 2008 financial crisis as it encouraged risk-taking by lenders who were able to quickly sell the debt on.

"The BoE has got good reasons for wanting to buy grade C assets but there's a risk that if they do too much then that can encourage bad lending. I think they probably ​understand ​that already," said William Allen, a visiting fellow at the National Institute of Economic and Social Research and a former ​head of the BoE's money markets division.

title: Wisconsin Cops Used Flock Over 100 Times To Track a Navy Veteran After He Lawfully Recorded a Traffic Stop
description: A federal lawsuit claims the Waukesha County Sheriff’s Office used the Flock cameras without a legitimate government purpose and in retaliation against the vet for exercising his First Amendment right...
fullText:
While standing in a private parking lot in Sussex, Wisconsin, on May 4, 2025, Napoleon Jones witnessed a traffic stop made by an out-of-county police officer. "It just didn't sit right with me," Jones told TMJ4 News, a local NBC News affiliate. "So I did what I legally could do, and I walked over and recorded it."

Jones, a United States Navy veteran, was well within his rights to record the police stop. But even though he recorded from a safe distance without interfering, that didn't stop the Waukesha County Sheriff's deputy, Brandon Shayhorn, from later unlawfully stopping and arresting Jones.

After Shayhorn completed the traffic stop, Jones returned to his vehicle. But before Jones could exit the parking lot, Shayhorn turned on his lights and initiated a second stop, claiming Jones' temporary license plate, displayed in the rearview window, was unreadable, reports TMJ4 News. Shayhorn demanded to see Jones' driver's license, but Jones refused, arguing that he'd been unlawfully pulled over on private property. Video clips of the encounter show the deputy opening Jones' door and pulling him from his vehicle.

Flock being used against a citizen in retaliation for exercising his first amendment right
-----

Jones was in a private parking lot across the street from a police officer he was recording on his phone. The officer saw him recording and came over and harassed him, pulled him… pic.twitter.com/bYAbmAeqwS

— Orwell Day (@OrwellDay) August 30, 2026

Jones was subsequently arrested "for resisting and obstructing," according to a federal lawsuit he filed against the arresting officers and police department. But after being held in custody for five hours, he was released with no citations or criminal charges. An internal post-arrest memorandum reviewed by Reason revealed that Shayhorn's supervisor informed him shortly after the arrest that he'd, in fact, illegally stopped Jones, and he therefore could not compel Jones to produce his identification.

The next day, Jones filed a citizen's complaint against Shayhorn for the illegal stop and said he believed Shayhorn retaliated against him for exercising his First Amendment right to record. Jones then sought legal counsel to pursue claims against the arresting officers and the police department for his unlawful stop, detention, and arrest.

While litigating those claims, Jones' attorney, Nate Cade, found something odd: A single photograph of his client's vehicle, provided by Flock Safety, dated May 30, 2025. Provided in the sheriff's office's response to Jones' complaint "was a single photograph of [Jones'] white vehicle, a white BMW," Cade told TMJ4 News. "The incident occurred on May 4, so that starts me thinking, what's going on? Why do you have a photograph of his vehicle 25 days later?" Cade continued.

Further investigation revealed over 100 Flock searches for a white BMW in the weeks following Jones' unlawful arrest. Some of the searches were made by Shayhorn himself, a clear conflict of interest. When asked about the searches during a deposition hearing, Shayhorn and others replied they'd been ordered to conduct the searches by their lieutenant in connection with Jones' citizen complaint, according to TMJ4 News.

"I was extremely shocked," Jones told TMJ4 News, "I couldn't understand why or how that would even be a possibility from what happened at the beginning of May would lead me to be searched in the Flock system because from my understanding, it's for criminal stuff."

In July 2026, Jones amended his complaint to include the additional officers who searched for his vehicle without "a legitimate law enforcement purpose" as required by the county's user agreement. There was no Flock camera in the parking lot where the unlawful arrest took place, and Jones was not accused nor suspected of any wrongdoing when the investigative searches took place. Indeed, Jones alleges that the officers instead used Flock to track Jones "in retaliation for exercising his First Amendment right of recording a traffic stop" and as a "means to attempt to find a potential crime against Jones."

At a time when police use of automated license plate readers is facing fierce public backlash for invading Americans' privacy, Jones' case serves as a reminder of just how easily government power can be abused without proper oversight. While the officers involved aren't being accused of attention-grabbing misuses of Flock Safety—like, say, using the tech to outlandishly stalk their romantic interests—their alleged abuses are still concerning. If lawfully filming a police officer can set off a weekslong surveillance campaign against the videographer, how can Americans expect other constitutionally protected speech and actions to not be met with similar retaliation?

The post Wisconsin Cops Used Flock Over 100 Times To Track a Navy Veteran After He Lawfully Recorded a Traffic Stop appeared first on Reason.com.

title: No Democrat has won a Kansas Senate seat in a century. Can a megachurch pastor change that?
description: Adam Hamilton has spent decades trying to bring people to Jesus as founder of the nation’s largest United Methodist church.  Now he wants to bring Kansas voters to the polls as the Democratic nominee ...
fullText:
EMPORIA, Kan. (AP) — Adam Hamilton has spent decades trying to bring people to Jesus as founder of the nation's largest United Methodist church. Now he wants to bring Kansas voters to the polls as the Democratic nominee for U.S. Senate.

A first-time candidate, Hamilton faces an unusual balancing act between political ambition and spiritual obligation. His pastoral role has given him rare prominence for a Democrat in a state where Republicans have won every Senate race for nearly a century, and some in his party are hoping for an upset victory over incumbent Sen. Roger Marshall.

But conservatives are also trying to use Hamilton's religious leadership against him. They suggest that his sermons prove he's too liberal for Kansas or even that he's a heretic for suggesting that non-Christians have a path to salvation after death.

Marshall said in an interview that Hamilton is "too woke for Kansas."

Hamilton isn't turning the other cheek. If Jesus were standing before them now, he said, "Roger Marshall would call him 'woke.'"

Only a few ordained ministers have served as senators over the past 100 years and just one — current Democrat Raphael Warnock of Georgia — remained an active pastor. If elected, Hamilton plans to continue as senior pastor at his Church of the Resurrection in the Kansas City area, preaching 12 to 18 times a year.

As Hamilton tries to win over center-right churchgoers as well as secular liberals, he's promising that he wouldn't use his perch in Washington to evangelize. He's on unpaid leave, going 11 weeks without giving a sermon this summer, although he peppers his remarks with biblical references, discusses Jesus' teachings with voters and spends several hours weekly on pastoral duties such as hospital visits.

"I need that interaction with people and the caring for people," he said after a meet-and-greet at a coffee shop in Emporia, a university town of 24,000 that's smaller than his congregation 110 miles (180 kilometers) to the northwest.

Hamilton, 61, built his church from a few members meeting in a funeral home chapel in 1990 into a 25,000-member congregation with nine locations across the Kansas City area. He's demonstrated an ability to raise money and has gained national attention by writing more than 30 books, mostly on Christian theology.

Hamilton describes himself as a centrist, running partly on "bringing people together." His congregation, he notes, is nearly evenly split between Democrats, Republicans and independents.

Republican-leaning Kansas has a sizable bloc of moderate voters, protects abortion rights and regularly elects Democratic governors. But Democrats haven't come within 10 points of winning a Senate race in more than 50 years, and they haven't won one since 1932.

Marshall, 66, is focused on rallying rural conservatives, a strategy that perennially works for Republicans. A fifth-generation farm kid who became an obstetrician, the senator is fluent in agriculture policy. He jibed that suburbanite Hamilton "doesn't know a heifer from a steer."

Marshall also warned that the Senate could fall under Democratic control if Hamilton wins the race.

"His party is too crazy for Kansas," Marshall said.

This year's race is unusual because of attacks from the Christian right branding Hamilton a heretic.

At issue is a 2022 sermon, reposted on X after Hamilton won the Democratic primary in August. Hamilton cited New Testament passages to argue that non-Christians can receive "the saving grace of Jesus" after death, avoiding eternal torment in Hell.

Republican Sen. Ted Cruz of Texas declared that Hamilton had rejected "the central tenets of Christianity," quoting a verse in the Gospel of John where Jesus declares, "No one comes to the Father except through me."

Marshall thanked Cruz for raising the issue, suggesting the sermon was "one of hundreds" of examples of Hamilton being out of step with Kansans.

Hamilton acknowledged that some Christians agree with Cruz — but cited other prominent Christians who might share his own view, including Methodist founder John Wesley and "Chronicles of Narnia" author C.S. Lewis.

"If he's going to call me a heretic, he's not the first," Hamilton said. "He won't be the last."

Hamilton also has faced skepticism from Democrats wary of mixing government with religion.

Republican conservatives routinely highlight their faith, suggesting that God wanted them to seek office and profusely thank God after winning.

This year during Lent — the 40 days of self-reflection and repentance before Easter — Hamilton said he skipped a meal each day and prayed about entering the Senate race.

"I'm never 100% sure about the will of God, so I tell people I am 87.2% sure I am supposed to be doing this," he said. "The Kansas voters will decide whether I'm supposed to win, but I feel like I was being called to step into the arena."

In Emporia, Hamilton said that as a senator, he'd "fight for the rights of all people, whether they have any faith or not."

"I'm not running for the Senate to make everybody in this country Christian or United Methodist," he said.

Nolan Guyer, a 72-year-old Navy veteran and retired nuclear plant operator, said he initially worried about voting for a minister, but Hamilton won him over enough that he donated to the pastor's campaign.

"I don't think it's the government's business to teach morals, and that is a preacher's job," Guyer said.

Republican political action committees have attacked Hamilton as so radical on climate change that he urged his congregation to repent for eating beef. They base that allegation on a misleading stitching together of two parts of a 2020 sermon, with one clip showing Hamilton calling Christians "to repentance" for not protecting God's creation and a second, earlier clip of him saying that "maybe changing your diet" is among personal actions that could reduce greenhouse gas emissions.

Another ad claimed that Hamilton's church helped pay for a drag queen story hour for children — a claim his campaign denies.

Marshall blamed Hamilton for a split in the United Methodist Church over allowing LGBTQ+ clergy, something it did in 2024. While Hamilton did support that change — at least since 2019 — he also had worked to prevent a split by backing a plan for a local option on whether to ordain or marry LGBTQ+ people.

Hamilton said his views on human sexuality and same-sex marriage evolved gradually, as he came to know gay and lesbian people in his congregation. His church now has a Queer Inclusive Collective ministry and participates in Pride events.

"One small part of my ministry has been trying to make sure that people who felt alienated from the church and pushed away knew that Christ welcomed them and they were loved by our congregation," Hamilton said.

One of Hamilton's assertions, that he is "running on decency," resonated with Jann Briggs. She's a retired teacher from Reading, a small town where the Methodist church is across the street from the Miracle Cafe.

Briggs and several friends came to Hamilton's event in Emporia with a copy of his latest book, "Holy Spirit: God's Presence and Power at Work in Us." He signed it for them.

"Finally, somebody who's speaking the right words," Briggs said.

Hamilton is also focusing on affordability, a key issue for Democrats this year. He has criticized Republican cuts to federal programs for the poor, such as food assistance and Medicaid coverage.

"I just want to know, when did it become 'woke' to care for your neighbor?" he asked.

fullText:
SINGAPORE/LONDON/NEW YORK, Sept 2 (Reuters) - Bond prices continued to slide in Asia and Europe on Wednesday, pushing borrowing costs to multi-decade highs as the Middle East conflict drives up energy prices and layers concerns about inflation on top of worries about ballooning government debt.

Sovereign bond yields are a reference point for asset prices across financial markets and the higher price of ‌money means elevated mortgage rates for consumers and tough choices for government spending as funding costs climb.

Japan's 10-year yield was perched above 3% for the first time in 30 years, while rising gas prices meant German ‌10-year Bund yields were stuck at their highest since 2011 and Britain's equivalent was at its highest since 2008. Yields rise as prices fall and vice versa.

A confluence of factors was at play, said State Street's head of macro strategy, Michael Metcalfe, with rising energy prices causing traders to bet ​on rate hikes, pushing up short-dated yields.

"The narrative is also getting wrapped up with longer-term concerns about the fiscal path. In France and the UK, we are going to get news on budgets soon. So, there are not many positives out there," Metcalfe said.

Bond sales from big tech companies aggressively raising money to fund the AI boom have added pressure on the sovereign bond market, as deep-pocketed U.S. tech firms compete with governments for investors' capital.

Naka Matsuzawa, chief macro strategist at Nomura Securities in Tokyo, said so-called hyperscalers' willingness to pay reasonably high rates was pulling up yields broadly, with the focus now on whether growth can rise along with them to help economies cope with the higher rates.

Yields can continue to rise as investors demand a higher premium, said ‌Charu Chanana, chief investment strategist at Saxo.

title: Deleted email details alleged Trump-targeting push inside Letitia James’ office: ‘Find and pursue crimes’
description: A prosecutor alleges Letitia James' bureau chief directed staff to target Donald Trump, Truth Social and other entities without credible reason.
fullText:
A New York prosecutor accused state Attorney General Letitia James' office of directing employees to "find and pursue crimes" involving President Donald Trump and entities tied to him, according to a report.

The allegation stems from an email sent by Assistant Attorney General Daniel Wiesenfeld, who works in the Investor Protection Bureau of the New York Office of the Attorney General, which is led by Shamiso Maswoswe, the Times Union reported. The email was allegedly later wiped from the office's servers, according to the outlet, while James' office dismissed the matter as a personnel issue and rejected claims that the office was targeting people based on political beliefs.

Wiesenfeld alleged that Maswoswe directed him to target "Trump himself, Truth Social, Hewlett Packard (DOJ approved merger)… without having a credible reason for targeting [these] organizations and individuals," according to the Times Union.

Maswoswe previously worked as a trial attorney in the Justice Department's Public Integrity Section from January 2016 until her termination in December 2017, under Trump's first term. In February 2021, she filed a discrimination lawsuit against the Justice Department, alleging she was unfairly terminated and subjected to discrimination based on her race, pregnancy and caregiving responsibilities.

Trump's Lawyers Put Dem Ag On Notice For Targeting His Family In Ny Fraud Fight: 'Cannot Stand'

Wiesenfeld reportedly sent an agency-wide email to colleagues Friday with instructions "to find and pursue crimes committed by specific individuals and organizations affiliated with Donald Trump," the Times Union reported.

The email reportedly was then allegedly wiped from servers, with a subsequent email sent from James' general counsel, Kumiki Gibson, informing employees that it was an "internal" matter and no employees were "in danger," the Times Union reported.

title: 'Below the dignity of the office': Canadian officials condemn Pete Hegseth cadet post
description: The US Defence Secretary is facing criticism for his apparent online mocking of members of Canada's cadet programme.
fullText:
US Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth is under fire in Canada for a social media post that appears to mock members of the country's cadet youth programme.

Hegseth posted the image, taken from the social media account for a local training branch, showing a young cadet receiving an award from her instructor.

He added a Canadian flag emoji and the caption "this is real" - an apparent attempt at disparaging Canada's military by making fun of the pair's appearance.

Canadian Defence Minister David McGuinty said on Tuesday that Hegseth's post was "below the dignity of the office".

The US and Canada are in the middle of a trade dispute that has often descended into a war of words, and the Trump administration has long accused their northern neighbour of relying on American military might for its defence.

Asked about the post and other recent jibes from Trump administration officials, Prime Minister Mark Carney said on Tuesday that any trade discussions would only begin again "when the Americans stop doing memes, stop throwing shade, stop trying to be tough and start being serious about having those discussions".

The Pentagon has said the post by Hegseth "speaks for itself".

The national cadet programme is overseen by the military and offers leadership and skills training to youth aged 12 to 18.

In a statement, the Army Cadet League of Canada, a civilian organisation that supports the programme, said it strongly condemns "any online harassment, or mockery of cadets' achievements".

"Directing derogatory commentary toward youth who are actively working to better themselves and serve their communities is unacceptable," the organisation said.

Speaking to broadcaster CBC, Canada's top military commander, General Jennie Carignan, said they are in contact with the cadets involved and any response they may have.

"We are consulting with them on how they want to go about doing this," she said.

Other officials weighed in, including Scott Anderson, a Conservative member of parliament for the Canadian city of Vernon and a former military reservist, who in a post directed at Hegseth accused him not living up to the "responsibility and decorum" that comes with his title.

"You have chosen to set both aside and insult two female Canadian non-combatants, and to intentionally shame them before millions. You should be ashamed," he said.

"Our economies, our continental defence and our cultures are irretrievably intertwined and yet we are two distinct nations. Canadians and Americans should have no problem with each other, but I have a problem with you," Anderson added.

A number of pundits and some Canadians accused the defence secretary of "body-shaming" with his post.

Trade talks broke down between Canada and the US last month, with both sides accusing the other of last-minute demands that torpedoed a tentative agreement.

The US immediately imposed 50% tariffs on some $20bn (C$28bn) of Canadian imports, and Canada plans to bring in matching countermeasures next week.

Both sides have traded insults, including Ontario Premier Doug Ford calling Trump a "loser", the US president seeking to change the name of Lake Ontario to Lake America, and transportation secretary Sean Duffy accusing Canada of being a country that "doesn't have a military".

Still, the two counties have long been defence partners and allies, including when Canada backed the US in the war in Afghanistan.

Canada has also significantly ramped up defence spending in recent months after years of lagging behind Nato targets.

Hegseth, a veteran, is himself under pressure at home following a string of recent high-profile military leaders leaving the Pentagon and questions about the US handling of the Iran war.

He has also long focused on the appearance and physical fitness of US troops and on what he calls the "warrior ethos".

title: Far-left writer ripped in viral debate over 'absurd' claim that capitalism is tied to White supremacy
description: Jemele Hill doubled down on her claim linking capitalism to White supremacy after a CNN panel clash with Kmele Foster over the issue.
fullText:
Liberal Atlantic writer Jemele Hill doubled down after suggesting that capitalism was linked to White supremacy, during a heated clash with another panelist on CNN on Tuesday.

"It's one thing to not think capitalism isn't working ideally. It's another thing entirely to insist that it is oppressive, that it is bound up with White supremacy," Kmele Foster, a podcast host, said.

The panelists were responding to newly unearthed 2020 comments, first reported by CNN, in which Texas Senate candidate James Talarico described capitalism as an "oppressive system" that is linked to White supremacy and climate change and needs to be dismantled.

Modern Capitalism Is Turning 250, Too. We Need To Remind Americans Why It's Important

"I've always preferred Adam Smith's description of capitalism as the natural system of liberty, the idea that people can own property, that they can exchange it freely with one another for profit, that they can find ways to put their resources to good use, those private property," Foster continued.

He added, "And profit in a way that is actually beneficial to everyone else, that there can be gains from trade that are mutually beneficial. These are foundational ideas that have created more wealth than any other system in human history. That is what capitalism is, that's not White supremacy."

"Do you think capitalism has always worked that way?" Hill asked Foster.

"I've actually just described the basic facts of economics," Foster responded. "Slavery is an institution that is older than writing. It predates capitalism. The notion that White supremacy and all these other things are bound up with capitalism in an intrinsic and fundamental way is so absurd and laughable, it barely needs to be defended."

Foster asked Hill to substantiate her argument and asked multiple times about the "the White supremacist dynamic of private property."

"But you're talking about capitalism in the purest form of how it was intended to work versus how it's actually working. It's not working," Hill argued.

Hill was called out on social media by other media commentators and hosts.

Political commentor Mary Katharine Ham said, "Kmele: 'You actually have to articulate what the connection is.' Hill writes for the Atlantic and has years of TV experience, but it didn't occur to her she would ever need to, and she isn't prepared to."

Podcast host Stephen Miller noted that Hill worked for the Atlantic and wrote, "She is a staff writer for one of the most prestigious neoliberal publications in the country and she's never been once challenged on any of her ideas like this."

Jemele Hill Falsely Claims Electoral College Is Entirely 'Rooted In Slavery' And It Cost Kamala The Election

Liberal commentator Leigh McGowan also made the case that capitalism was not working during the exchange.

"I think that's the problem. I think the problem is it's not working well, today. I think for a long time that is a great way to describe it. Adam Smith capitalism, if we had that, that would be totally different," she said. "We have got to a place where we have deregulated everything so much that only a certain handful of people are actually succeeding in this version of capitalism."

Socialism has gained popularity among younger voters, according to a Fox News Poll from March. The survey found a record 38% believed it would be a good thing for the United States to move away from capitalism and in the direction of socialism — up from 32% in 2022, the last time the question was asked. In 2010, a low of 18% backed socialism.

Hill appeared to double down after the exchange.

"America was built on the institution of slavery. It is how America became a world economic power — the buying and selling of people being tied to the economy. That is effectively White supremacy, since it was a race-based system. Fast-forward to other economic policies that were guided by race — housing, employment, etc. There were rules that prevented Black people from equally participating in the free economy. In fact, one of the most glaring features of American capitalism is racial inequality. The racial wealth gap exists because specific policies were put in place to suppress economic participation. So yes, capitalism is tied to White supremacy," Hill said in a post to X that followed the CNN panel debate.

Hill did not immediately respond to Fox News Digital's request for further comment.

Talarico made his 2020 comments at the Austin Sierra Club during a virtual candidate forum while serving his first term as a state representative. His answer came in response to a question about what lawmakers could do to address climate change in communities of color, according to CNN's K-File.

"I am so thankful that you asked this question and also thankful that young activists have really drawn the link between climate change and White supremacy and capitalism in our country," Talarico said. "And I think only ending the ways that all three of those oppressive systems work together are we gonna be able to begin the process of dismantling them."

During the same event, Talarico said the oil and gas industry was not going to last.

"We all know that Texas has been a leader in oil and gas, but in many ways that's like being the leader in cassette tapes in the 1980s," Talarico later said, responding to another question. "That industry is not gonna last. And if we wanna ensure we have an economy that's gonna work for our children and our children's children, we gotta be ahead of the curve and Texas has to lead instead of follow on this issue."

"James supports the oil and gas industry and believes in an all of the above energy strategy that protects Texas oil and gas jobs. He's already said he missed the mark on some of his past statements, but Ken Paxton is clipping a few old, cringey comments to distract from his career of corruption that includes being impeached by his own party, enriching himself and his billionaire mega-donors, and using his office to protect pedophiles and animal abusers," Talarico campaign spokesperson JT Ennis told Fox News Digital in a statement regarding the oil and gas industry remarks.

Ennis' statement also said Talarico is a "proud capitalist," and "agrees with the majority of Texans that racism, natural disasters, and a billionaire-controlled economy are all problems we need to address."

"James has already said he missed the mark on some of his past statements, while Ken Paxton has refused to address his comments that the school shooting in Uvalde was 'God's plan' and that Texas' abortion ban is good for interstate commerce," the statement continued.

The Democratic state representative is facing off against Republican Ken Paxton in the midterm elections for U.S. Senate in November.

title: Council plans next step in city expansion fight
description: Council leader Dan Harrison says the government needs to explain why it has drawn up new boundaries.
fullText:
Leicestershire County Council has said it is to take the next step towards a potential legal challenge to plans to expand Leicester.

The Reform UK-led authority said it was concerned that some 250,000 people currently living in the county face being moved within the boundary of an enlarged Leicester council from 2028.

Council leader Dan Harrison said he planned to send a "pre-action protocol" letter to the government asking for the reasoning and evidence supporting the decision it announced in July.

Harrison, who described the coming expansion of the city as "heartbreaking", said the government's response could determine whether the council pursues a judicial review.

The city expansion is part of the Labour government's plan to reshape the political map of Leicestershire and Rutland by replacing 10 existing councils with two new local authorities.

The Ministry of Housing, Communities and Local Government (MHCLG) has been asked for comment.

It previously said the process, known as local government reorganisation (LGR), would improve public services, create larger, more financially sustainable councils, and provide land needed for new homes to accommodate Leicester's growing population.

Speaking to the BBC's East Midlands political editor Peter Saull, Andy Burnham previously said he would consider people's concerns.

"I'm always prepared to look again at issues and coming in, three weeks in, I will take a look at the consultation and the responses, and I know sometimes these changes are not easy," the prime minister said.

He added the structure of local government in Greater Manchester, where he was the regional mayor before becoming prime minister, allowed him to "drive growth and change".

"If we want to give maximum devolved powers to all parts of the East Midlands, I think we do need to see reforms to local government," he said.

"This is not a step we would take lightly," Harrison said.

"But creating a larger city is the single biggest change for Leicestershire in living memory.

"The people of Leicestershire are entitled to transparency about a decision which could reshape their communities and local services for generations."

The government has been accused of ignoring the result of its own consultation on the changes, which showed 87% of some 6,600 responses opposed city expansion.

Harrison added: "We stand firmly with our residents.

"They've spoken loud and clear about the Government's flawed decision and we cannot ignore the strength of feeling across the communities affected.

"Dozens of towns and villages face being swallowed up by a city expansion and we must do everything we can to protect their character and future services."

The Conservative and Liberal Democrat opposition groups at County Hall have also backed the sending of the letter.

The sole Green Party councillor on the county council also opposed the city expansion during a vote on it last month.

Tory group leader Deborah Taylor said: "At last month's council meeting, we made it clear that we were united in defence of our county against a city land grab.

"We stand squarely behind our residents in this fight."

Leader of the council's Liberal Democrat group Michael Mullaney said: "We will continue to fight the government's disgraceful plan to drag hundreds of thousands of county residents into Leicester City.

"We've always said this is a disastrous plan for communities and we support the county council's challenge."

Under the move, once the city boundary is widened, the rest of the county and Rutland will be served by a single unitary council called Leicestershire and Rutland Council. It will mean the existing seven district councils will cease to exist from the point the new structure is in place in April 2028.

Leicester's Labour mayor Sir Peter Soulsby pushed for an expansion to the city boundary which he said was long overdue.

He previously said: "It's the right thing for the city because Leicester, Nottingham, Derby... we lost out in the 1970s when most similar cities saw their boundaries massively extended.

"We were kept within 19th Century boundaries and the change is something that frankly before the announcement privately all of the local parties were very much recognising was the necessity.

"It's going to happen and I think what matters now is that we get on with making it happen in a way that enables the people of Leicester and the surrounding area to have their services preserved."

Soulsby added: "It's also very important to say that what this does is to enable the people around Leicester who are very much a part of the greater Leicester area to have a say in the governance of their city.

"They'll have a vote, they will have a stake in the city of which they are effectively already a part."

The mayor told the BBC he did not anticipate a "massive hike" in council tax for residents brought within the city boundary.

"In fact, it's quite the contrary," he added.

"Because studies that have been jointly undertaken between the city and the county council show that there is the potential saving, the likely saving of over £40m a year for local council taxpayers as a result of these changes."

title: Oakland coffee shop accused of kicking out Jewish dad, 5-year-old son and shutters amid antisemitism lawsuits
description: Jerusalem Coffee House faces a federal civil rights trial after the Justice Department alleged the Oakland cafe refused service to Jewish customers.
fullText:
Jerusalem Coffee House in Oakland, California, remained closed Wednesday after temporarily shutting its doors last week to focus on three lawsuits alleging it discriminated against Jewish customers, including a father and his 5-year-old son. The Palestinian-owned café is preparing for an October federal civil rights trial.

The coffeehouse announced in August that it would stop operating after Aug. 23 while its owners prepared for the litigation, including a Justice Department case scheduled for trial Oct. 26.

A federal judge previously rejected the defendants' attempt to dismiss the DOJ lawsuit, which alleges Fathi Abdulrahim Harara and employees refused service to Jewish customers wearing Star of David caps and followed them outside while hurling insults and threats.

The café blamed its legal problems on efforts to suppress its pro-Palestinian politics in an August statement on Substack, announcing the closure.

Doj Investigating Nyc Coffee Shop Over Hostile Social Post About Pro-israel Politician

"These lawsuits represent the ongoing efforts of Zionist organizations and the federal government to use the courts as a tool to repress free speech and public political commitments to Palestine," it said.

Elizabeth Barcohana, the California Republican Party Jewish engagement chair and an attorney, criticized the shop's defense of its conduct in a statement to Fox News Digital Wednesday.

"It is ironic that after freely expressing support for terrorism with these beverage names, the café owners appear to now be using the First Amendment as a defense for ejecting two Jewish customers who wore hats with Stars of David on them, in one case calling it a 'violent' hat," she said.

"By their own standard, if a hat can be violent, so can an iced tea. The First Amendment protects speech on hats; it does NOT protect businesses open to the public to discriminate against its customers because they're Jews while chasing them in the street shouting 'Jew' at them.

Hamas, Hezbollah Flags Fly At Anti-israel Protest Minutes After Mamdani Condemns Terror Plot Against Jews

"On the one-year anniversary of October 7th, a Palestinian terrorist attack against innocent civilians that killed over 1,200 people and took hundreds of hostages including children and Americans, Jerusalem Coffee Shop in Oakland unveiled a new menu celebrating terrorism. Beverage items named 'Iced in Tea Fada' celebrate Intifada (an Arabic call to violence signifying resistance by any means necessary, including terrorism) and 'Sweet Sinwar' honoring the principal architect behind the attack," she added.

The coffee shop co-founder previously denied that "Sweet Sinwar" referred to the Hamas leader and said the menu's Oct. 7 rollout coincided with the business's anniversary rather than the anniversary of the Hamas attack, according to The San Francisco Standard.

Barcohana said she hoped the current shutdown would become permanent.

"The owners have temporarily closed the coffee shop while they defend this discrimination lawsuit against them," she said. "Hopefully it remains permanently closed."

The Justice Department filed its case in June 2025 under Title II of the Civil Rights Act of 1964.

The Anti-Defamation League and Benesch sued on behalf of Michael Radice, who alleges he was refused service and subjected to antisemitic slurs, while the Louis D. Brandeis Center filed a state lawsuit on behalf of Jonathan Hirsch, who was ejected with his young son after Harara confronted him over his Star of David hat.

When the Justice Department announced its case, Assistant Attorney General Harmeet K. Dhillon of the Civil Rights Division said federal public-accommodation laws applied regardless of the business's political views.

"Through our vigorous enforcement of Title II of the Civil Rights Act and other laws prohibiting race and religious discrimination, the Justice Department is committed to combatting antisemitism and discrimination and protecting the civil rights of all Americans."

title: 'Alexa for Shopping' Can Now Help You Spot a Spam Email
description: Amazon's AI might be able to confirm whether or not the company is messaging you.
fullText:
While many internet scams are obvious enough to easily avoid, they are growing more sophisticated. Even seasoned users may find themselves duped by a clever fake email, text, or phone call. Case in point: If you receive a message from "Amazon," you might have trouble quickly identifying whether or not it's legitimate. That could lead you to either fall for a trap, or, if the message is real, miss an important announcement or alert from the company.

There are plenty of tactics and best practices out there for verifying these messages on your own, of course: You can take a look at the email address or phone number that sent it, and do your own research to see whether it's official contact info for the company (depending on the email address, this might be apparent on its own); you can study the body of the message, looking for grammar and spelling mistakes that would give away a hasty phishing scheme; and you can note any financial requests, or time-sensitive demands, which would raise the stakes and increase the chances that someone would treat the message and its contents as legitimate.

But none of these tactics allows you to confirm directly with the company—in this case, Amazon—whether that outreach is real. A new Alexa tool does just that.

On Wednesday, Amazon announced an interesting new initiative aimed at reducing—if not eliminating—the risk of users falling for scams. Starting today, "Alexa for Shopping," Amazon's shopping assistant, will help you verify whether an email, text, or phone call from "Amazon" is actually from the company. The company says you can ask Alexa for Shopping questions like "Did Amazon send me a text about a delivery problem yesterday?" "Is this email about my Prime membership from Amazon real?" or "I got a call about a refund from someone saying they're from Amazon. Was that real?” In addition, you ask Alexa for Shopping 

The AI will use these details to figure out whether the message is something Amazon sent itself. What's unique about this new feature is that the bot can actually check your details against the company's record of "every communication it has sent," including sender information, message content, when messages were sent, and exact formatting. Amazon says it completes this check "within seconds," and you'll receive one of the following answers: confirmed from Amazon, not from Amazon, or unable to verify. Amazon says Alexa for Shopping will only confirm a message is real if it has total certainty.

If the message was from Amazon, the company will confirm that the message type, source, date, and time were all consistent with Amazon's message records. You'll also get tips for keeping your account secure—whether you asked for them or not. If the message is not from Amazon, you might get a result like, “This message does not appear to match any official Amazon communication based on the information provided.” Alexa for Shopping may then follow up with recommendations, like checking your orders in the app, contacting Amazon directly, and warnings against clicking links or replying to the message. If it can't confirm the message, Amazon may encourage you to try another verification method.

This isn't the first verification method Amazon has rolled out. The company says it launched an email address, "[email protected]," earlier this year for users to forward messages to. There is also an existing Amazon customer service form that walks you through filing a similar request. Alexa for Shopping will likely point you in these directions if it can't verify your message for whatever reason.

While companies continue to shove AI features into all of their products, this one from Amazon seems potentially quite useful. It's such a simple concept that I'm surprised more companies don't already offer a similar service. Why not automatically check user submissions against your message records to help separate real messages from spam? Perhaps Amazon will be a trailblazer here—assuming the feature actually works, and doesn't hallucinate verifications.

title: Woltemade move underlines summer of change at Newcastle
description: It was ultimately a tale of two very different forwards on deadline day as Nick Woltemade left Newcastle United to join Juventus on loan and the club announced the arrival of Matias Fernandez-Pardo.
fullText:
It was rather telling that Matias Fernandez-Pardo was Newcastle United's final signing of a rollercoaster summer.

This was a pursuit which was anything but straightforward.

The Belgian had been Newcastle's top target before the window opened, but it was only in the final stages of the summer that the club were able to complete a complex deal following delicate negotiations with Lille.

It was ultimately a tale of two very different forwards on deadline day.

On the same afternoon Newcastle announced the rapid Fernandez-Pardo's arrival, towering club-record signing Nick Woltemade finalised his loan move to Juventus.

Woltemade only joined Newcastle last summer, but this has been a window of change on Tyneside.

Head coach Eddie Howe stepped down in July and was replaced by Matthias Jaissle just a few weeks before the start of the new campaign.

Captain Bruno Guimaraes was among a handful of key players to leave while eight new signings arrived as Newcastle's records for spending and sales in a single window were both smashed.

This was the summer which altered the face of the club.

A shake-up had been signposted as far back as the spring.

It was in early April when Newcastle announced that defender Kieran Trippier would be leaving at the end of his contract.

The 34-year-old was approaching the twilight of his career, but his departure was still keenly felt as an influential figure behind the scenes.

"It was emotional for me, of course, because I loved the club so much and Newcastle gave me so much in return," the former England international said several months after moving on to Wolves.

"I'll always follow the club and want them to do well but, as a footballer, sometimes, you have to move on. With the utmost respect, I think it was the right time for both the club and myself.

"As I've always said, I wanted to leave in the right manner and show respect to my team-mates, the club and, most importantly, the supporters, who I have a great relationship with."

Anthony Gordon and Sandro Tonali's subsequent exits to Barcelona and Tottenham respectively did not necessarily come as a surprise, either, given they enabled Newcastle to comply and reinvest within the game's financial rules.

No-one internally had countenanced losing talisman Guimaraes, though.

However, having bailed Newcastle out so many times before, even the tireless midfielder dropped to the turf, untied his boots before the physio reached him and glared at the bench to come off during last season's final-day defeat at Fulham.

If ever an image summed up a bruising domestic campaign as Newcastle finished in 12th place - far below where the hierarchy had projected - and missed out on millions worth of European revenue.

The prospect of Guimaraes signing a new deal was unsurprisingly shot down by a figure involved in his subsequent £75m move to Arsenal a few weeks later.

After losing Alexander Isak to Liverpool against their wishes last summer, Newcastle ended up selling a fourth key player in less than a year.

They also missed out on top targets Victor Munoz and Johan Manzambi, who opted to move to Liverpool and Aston Villa respectively.

Yet those inside the club repeatedly stressed that the window could only be judged once it shut.

"Just because one element doesn't go the way you want doesn't mean you abandon the plan," a senior source said.

"We stayed on target, stayed focused, stayed calm and moved on. We didn't do a whole lot of mourning or crying when we had a setback.

The final fortnight of the summer ultimately proved critical as defender Amar Dedic, midfielder Nico Gonzalez and forward Matias Fernandez-Pardo all joined the club.

Season ticket holder Adam Widdrington believes the trio's arrivals and Newcastle's performances in the 2-2 draw against Liverpool and the 2-0 win at Tottenham Hotspur changed the narrative.

"Plenty of pundits and other fans had Newcastle earmarked for relegation," he said.

"They said, 'Who's the manager? Never heard of him. Who are these young players? You have lost a load of players'.

"I still wouldn't class it as a great transfer window, but I think it's a good one, especially given the context of where it looked like Newcastle were heading in that Bruno dip.

"At that point, it didn't feel like there was so much to inspire the fans, but the last three signings shifted opinion a lot."

Fernandez-Pardo certainly feels more of a stylistic fit for a side who made the most sprints in the opening weekend (138) of the Premier League season.

Jaissle has already cited the forward's "explosiveness" which, for all his endeavour, was not part of Woltemade's game, even during an impressive start to his Newcastle career a year ago.

Fernandez-Pardo will have to quickly adapt and there will inevitably be ups and downs as the campaign progresses for the 21-year-old and a young side.

"We always have hope and belief," Jaissle said before a ball had even been kicked this season. "No one can take that away from us."

title: Defending champion Murphy exits British Open
description: Defending champion Shaun Murphy is knocked out of the British Open after a 4-2 defeat to David Gilbert in the second round.
fullText:
Defending champion Shaun Murphy has been knocked out of the British Open after a 4-2 defeat to David Gilbert in the second round.

Gilbert made a break of 117 to win the opening frame before fellow Englishman Murphy took the next two with break of 64 and 103.

However, Gilbert peeled off three more half-centuries in the next three frames to secure his place in the last 32 in Cheltenham.

New world number one Zhao Xintong held off a fightback from Welshman Daniel Wells – who had been 3-0 down – to progress 4-2.

Judd Trump rattled off breaks of 96 and 87 as he came from behind to clinch a 4-2 win over Ricky Walden.

China's Bai Yulu narrowly lost her match against Ross Muir in a last-frame decider, having looked set for victory after a break of 59.

John Higgins edged to a 4-3 victory against Noppon Saengkham while Stan Moody beat Yao Pengcheng 4-1.

Elsewhere, Mark Selby also won a last-frame decider against Lei Peifan in the morning and then returned in the evening session to repeat the feat against Jackson Page in the third round.

title: Birds stop play but Medvedev flies into third round
description: An interruption from a pair of birds ruffles Daniil Medvedev's feathers but fails to disrupt the seventh seed as he eases into the US Open third round with a dominant victory over Sebastian Gorzny.
fullText:
An interruption from a pair of birds ruffled Daniil Medvedev's feathers but could not disrupt the seventh seed as he eased into the US Open third round with a dominant victory over Sebastian Gorzny.

The two birds settled down on the net for a closer look at the action midway through a second-set rally, with play continuing around them for several strokes before the chair umpire called for the point to be replayed.

Medvedev, who placed the incident in his "top five" most unusual experiences at the New York major, was visibly stunned by the decision which came just after he thought he had won the point with a cross-court forehand.

"This is very bad," the 2021 champion said as he remonstrated at the umpire on court.

Russia's Medvedev is no stranger to losing his composure on court, notably receiving a fine of almost £31,500 at last year's US Open for an extraordinary meltdown during his first-round defeat to Benjamin Bonzi.

As recently as last month's Winston-Salem Open, where he again lost in the opening round, he spent a disconsolate change of ends questioning his future in the sport, musing "maybe I should start a career in pickleball".

However, the 30-year-old, who had already flown through the first set in just 21 minutes, quickly brushed aside the avian interruption to complete a straightforward 6-1 6-3 7-5 win over American wildcard Gorzny, the world number 731.

"I saw [the birds] straight away," Medvedev - who will play Frenchman Arthur Rinderknech in the third round - said in his on-court interview.

"I thought the point would stop straight away but it didn't.

"Then we play for 45 seconds and the moment I hit the winner we say stop. I'm like, 'Why? We played for 45 seconds!'.

"But it's okay. I was not happy with the decision but it is was it is. You can't do anything with it.

"The situation was pretty crazy but I love this court, I'm happy to win, to stay in the US Open, to stay in New York for longer."

Gorzny was making his Grand Slam debut at the US Open, seven years after being given a 5% chance to live after being taken ill at the USTA Boys' 16s National Championships in Michigan.

Then aged 15, Gorzny suffered a seizure in the night and was placed in an induced coma for four days.

"The doctors aren't really sure what it was actually, but they're guessing a mosquito bite that led to some type of brain infection: meningitis, encephalitis," Gorzny told the ATP before the US Open.

A former Wimbledon boys' doubles champion, Gorzny, the world number 731, earned his place in the main draw at Flushing Meadows by winning the USTA American Collegiate Player Wildcard Playoff in June.

title: Carse left out of England squad for third Pakistan Test
description: England leave Brydon Carse out of their squad for the third and final Test against Pakistan at Edgbaston.
fullText:
England have omitted Brydon Carse from their squad for the third and final Test against Pakistan at Edgbaston.

The 31-year-old Durham seamer was dropped for the second Test at Lord's after he was briefly arrested following an incident outside a Derby nightclub on 22 August.

Derbyshire police are continuing to investigate an allegation of assault in connection with that incident.

Carse's replacement, 23-year-old Sonny Baker, has retained his place in England's 15-man party.

Surrey's Matthew Fisher has been dropped from an otherwise unchanged England squad as they seek to complete a series clean-sweep over Pakistan.

The third Test in Birmingham starts on Wednesday, 9 September at 11:00 BST.

With six white-ball matches against Sri Lanka to follow the Test series, England may consider resting seamers Jofra Archer, Gus Atkinson and Josh Tongue, all of whom feature in the limited-overs set-up.

While the trio have been named in the Test squad, they may be rotated in favour of Baker, Essex pace bowler Sam Cook and Derbyshire spinner Shoaib Bashir.

Cook, 29, played his one Test against Zimbabwe last summer while 22-year-old Bashir is yet to feature in this series, with England preferring an all-pace attack.

Baker made his only Test appearance to date in a much-changed line-up against New Zealand at The Oval in June.

Carse remains available for selection for Durham and finished with match figures of 4-95 in their win over Gloucestershire last week.

However, he has not been picked in the XI for their match against Northamptonshire, which started on Wednesday.

Pakistan made the extraordinary move of dropping seven players, calling up five uncapped players and releasing their head coach prior to the Edgbaston Test.

Sarfaraz Ahmed has replaced by Pakistan white-ball coach Mike Hesson, while Muhammad Rizwan, Imam-ul-Haq, Salman Ali Agha, Ali Usman and Khurram Shahzad, all of whom have featured in the series, are among the players dropped.

England beat Pakistan by an innings and 103 runs in the first Test at Headingley and sealed series victory with a win by 194 runs at Lord's last week.

title: LA Clippers fined $30m by NBA over Leonard scandal
description: The LA Clippers are fined $30m (£22.2m) by the NBA for violating salary rules over the acquisition of star player Kawhi Leonard.
fullText:
The LA Clippers have been fined $30m (£22.2m) by the National Basketball Association (NBA) for violating salary rules in order to funnel millions of dollars to star player Kawhi Leonard.

The fine - the largest in the league's history - comes after the NBA report said Leonard pressured the Clippers into "obtaining off-court income opportunities [and] successfully obtaining those opportunities".

The Clippers will also have to forfeit five first-round draft picks between 2029 and 2033, while owner Steve Ballmer has been suspended from all league and team activities for 12 months for his role in matters involving Leonard's sponsorship contracts during his time with the franchise.

The NBA said the Clippers had been guilty of "knowingly seeking to help Mr Leonard obtain off-court income opportunities".

NBA commissioner Adam Silver said he was "deeply disappointed" by the Clippers' "flagrant violations" of the rules and said he believed the "severity of the penalties reflects the seriousness of the violations".

Two-time NBA champion Leonard has been fined $700,000 (£518,997) by the league.

The team's president of business operations, Gillian Zucker, has been suspended for one year without pay for providing "misleading statements to investigators".

The punishments come after the NBA said its month-long investigation "found a pattern of misconduct and multiple significant rules violations by the Clippers organisation, a prior offender of the salary-cap circumvention rules".

Following the ruling, Leonard, 35, said he "accepts full responsibility" for his actions and "regrets the distraction this situation has caused the fans and my family".

"I entered into my contract with the Clippers as well as the agreements in question in good faith, fully committed to fulfilling my obligations and with no knowledge of any intent on anyone's part to circumvent the salary cap," he wrote on Instagram.

The two-time NBA Finals MVP joined the Clippers in 2019 and spent seven years with the franchise before leaving earlier this year.

The NBA said both the "organisation and personnel" of the Clippers will be subject to a compliance and monitoring programme overseen by the league for five years.

title: Boulter wins one game in 58-minute US Open defeat
description: British number one Katie Boulter is dumped out in the second round of the US Open as she wins just one game in a 58-minute demolition by Karolina Muchova.
fullText:
British number one Katie Boulter endured a "bad day at the office" as she won just one game in a 58-minute demolition by Wimbledon runner-up Karolina Muchova in the US Open second round.

The match, originally scheduled to be played on one of the outer courts, was moved to the 14,000-capacity Louis Armstrong Stadium after heavy rain in New York.

But fans who had counted themselves lucky to have gained a third match on their day session ticket may have been left feeling short-changed, as Boulter fell to a swift 6-1 6-0 defeat by the Czech seventh seed.

"Ultimately, it was a bad day at the office – times two," said Boulter.

"I struggled with the conditions. I struggled with the roof, the noise, I let things distract me.

"I let it get to me. I'm not usually aware of everything going on. It made me feel a little bit uncomfortable. I have to deal with it better."

Fellow Britons Jacob Fearnley and Toby Samuel failed to reach the men's third round on Wednesday, both losing to seeded players in Argentina's Tomas Martin Etcheverry and Jiri Lehecka of the Czech Republic.

But Francesca Jones had better fortune as she returned to win her first-round match against Poland's Magda Linette after it was interrupted by rain on Tuesday.

Boulter's serve let her down as she hit eight double faults and no aces, while she won just 33% of points behind her first serve.

Unable to fend off any of the seven break points she faced, the 30-year-old was not helped by an unforced error count of 22 compared to just four winners.

In comparison, two-time US Open semi-finalist Muchova landed 14 winners and just nine unforced errors as she impressed with smart drop shots and piercing groundstrokes.

"I would be really humbled [if I was Boulter], I would sit down with my team and say 'OK, we need to change something big time'," former world number five Daniela Hantuchova told BBC Radio 5 Live.

"First of all, it was very obvious today that it was the serve. I feel like it needs to be cleared up because she was losing the rhythm and not using her legs. That's the number one thing.

"If I am Boulter, I would be on the practice court tomorrow. If she still wants to invest everything into her tennis then she needs to be on the court."

Boulter has had plenty to celebrate in her personal life this summer after marrying Australia's Alex de Minaur, the world number seven, in July.

However, it has been a disappointing tennis season for the world number 62, with just two wins across the four Grand Slam tournaments.

Since suffering a first-round exit at Wimbledon, Boulter has won just two of the six matches she has played.

Birds stop play but Medvedev flies into third round

Jones had won the first set 6-4 against Linette, ranked 82nd, when the rain put a halt to proceedings on Tuesday night.

When the pair returned on Wednesday, it was Linette who appeared fresher as she raced to a 5-0 lead and wrapped up the second set in 28 minutes.

"I've never been quite in this position so I was nervous with how I'd quite feel about coming back out," Jones told Sky Sports afterwards.

"I thought I'd maybe handle it better than the score reflects."

Jones rallied back in the decider, claiming the decisive break at 2-1 before completing the victory - just her second at Grand Slam level.

She will play American 14th seed Iva Jovic in the second round on Thursday.

"[I'm] really grateful that I just managed to pull through," said Jones.

"She came out all guns blazing - it was incredible how she was playing until about 4-0 and then it started to equal out. But in that situation, hats off if they can sustain that, I just tried to show my northern grit, stick in there and do what I can."

Fearnley had produced a remarkable five-set comeback against Spain's Martin Landaluce in the first round, but the British lucky loser's fortune ran out in a 6-3 6-3 3-6 6-3 defeat by against Etcheverry.

The Argentine 27th seed recovered from losing the third set and falling a break behind in the fourth, while Fearnley's 57 unforced errors and 11 double faults ultimately proved costly.

Samuel, 23, won through qualifying to reach round two on his US Open debut, but was beaten 6-4 6-2 6-4 by 18th seed Lehecka.

Meanwhile, British number three Jan Choinski fell to a 6-3 6-1 7-6 (7-5) defeat by Dutchman Botic van de Zandschulp in a first-round match that had also been pushed back to Wednesday because of the rain.

title: Fury calls Joshua a 'coward' as wait for announcement continues
description: Tyson Fury says Anthony Joshua is a "coward" as the pair face a tense wait to see whether their long-awaited all-British heavyweight blockbuster can be agreed.
fullText:
Tyson Fury has labelled Anthony Joshua a "coward" as the pair face a tense wait to see whether their long-awaited all-British heavyweight bout can be agreed.

The long-time rivals had been expected to finally settle their differences and face off in November, but the likelihood of that happening is diminishing as an agreement over the venue has yet to be reached.

Two-time unified world champion Joshua and his Matchroom promoter Eddie Hearn have signed a contract for the fight to take place in the United Kingdom, while the fight's organisers are understood to favour staging it in the United States.

Hearn has previously said the contracts would have to be renegotiated if the fight were to take place outside the United Kingdom.

On Wednesday, Fury, who defeated journeyman Mariusz Wach last month to keep the potential blockbuster clash with Joshua on track, said negotiations over the fight were becoming "quite tiring".

"I've been down to fight at every location that's been mentioned - England, Ireland, Vegas, New York, back to England, back to Ireland, back to New York," said the 38-year-old.

"Listen, I've said yep, yep, yep, yep, yep, every single time. Zero stipulations.

"The facts are I feel like you're being a coward. I feel like you don't want the fight and you're just conning everybody. I feel like you've been doing that for years.

"You've had many opportunities to fight me, but deep down you've never really wanted it, so let's see if you're going to man up for a final time."

In a separate post, Fury continued to taunt Joshua, 36, this time alongside former heavyweight champion Mike Tyson, telling his fellow Brit to "sign the contract, big boy" as he paid homage to Tyson's iconic line.

Queensbury's Frank Warren, who promotes Fury, told Sky Sports News his fighter was "100%" signed up for the fight.

"It is signed by Tyson," said Warren. "Tyson is signed up for the fight and agreed for the fight."

title: Late-night transfer fallout sparks Chelsea-Monaco row
description: How Chelsea, Everton and Monaco all missed out after late-night drama on deadline day. Nizaar Kinsella reports.
fullText:
One source with connections to both Chelsea and Monaco said the clubs had "played with fire and got burned".

Indeed, the late-night transfer drama that involved Folarin Balogun, Everton, Monaco, Lamine Camara and Chelsea saw all parties lose out.

Camara - a 22-year-old Senegalese international midfielder - had been a target for Chelsea as they prepared for the £125m sale of Enzo Fernandez to Manchester City.

But Monaco were adamant he was going nowhere for the fee Chelsea were willing to pay.

"I've been speaking to them for the last 10 days," said Monaco sporting director Thiago Scuro said.

"At around 16:00 BST yesterday we got contact from Chelsea. The answer was the same: no."

Instead, the Ligue 1 club had allowed United States international striker Balogun, 25, to fly to Merseyside to complete a £40m move to Everton. According to Monaco, Camara had agreed to stay with the club.

With three hours remaining of the transfer window, Chelsea were content with their midfield options, despite the sale of Fernandez, after failing with enquiries for Camara and Roma's Manu Kone.

But issues with Balogun's Everton medical presented an opportunity for Chelsea.

"Of course, Chelsea saw an opportunity," Scuro added.

"'Monaco need money, Balogun is struggling there, let's go and try.' Chelsea called us and said: 'Maybe we can be the solution.'

"At that moment, we had to open the door to discussions."

Negotiations were back underway with Monaco at 20:00 BST and a £47m fee was agreed shortly after.

Meanwhile, Everton failed to find alternatives to Balogun and revived their move with minutes before the deadline.

Chelsea had completed all the necessary paperwork for Camara and did not need to submit a deal sheet - a request to the Premier League for additional time to complete a transfer, post the deadline.

But the plug was pulled. Monaco acknowledge Camara was disappointed after he had spoken to manager Xabi Alonso, passed a medical and signed a contract until 2033.

"What happened was that around 22:00 BST our time, maybe a bit earlier, Everton realised there was no issue and decided they were ready to sign the contract [for Balogun]," Scuro told reporters on Wednesday afternoon.

"As soon as we received that information, we came back to Chelsea and said there was no deal. Because that's also fair. It's part of the game."

Chelsea were left furious, claiming Monaco informed them in writing that the deal would not proceed rather than communicating the decision by phone.

Monaco thought - by signing a deal sheet, five minutes before the 23:00 BST deadline, to allow Everton extra time to complete the transfer of Balogun - they had secured the sale they needed to help comply with Uefa's financial regulations.

The Ligue 1 side were under pressure to generate 150m euros in player sales this summer, and had raised 106m euros from departures.

Another twist was still to come.

In the early hours of Tuesday morning, the former Arsenal striker had a change of heart which saw him leave Everton's Finch Farm training ground without signing for the club.

Scuro claims Balogun felt he was mistreated while at Everton's training ground, something the Premier League club disputes.

"We had to respect his decision," Scuro added.

"We found solutions, challenged the medical assessment and worked through the issues.

"I don't want to create a war with Chelsea or Everton.

"My role is to protect Monaco and act in the club's best interests. That's what I've done since I arrived.

"It's not about being loved by people outside the club. It's about doing what Monaco needs."

Scuro says it is possible Monaco will look at selling other players to countries whose transfer window remains open in order to acquire the funds they need.

The Monaco chief is open to welcoming back both players. Camara has already returned to training and is set to feature in their upcoming match away at Paris St-Germain on Friday night.

"I really understand because a player can get excited by conversations with a coach and by everything a club like Chelsea can offer," Scuro continued.

"This is not the end of the world. It's one opportunity. For a player with his level of talent, I'm very confident he will soon have even better options and offers than the one he had yesterday."

According to sources close to Camara, Liverpool also retain a long-standing interest in a future deal.

Chelsea had been considering Camara as an option to replace Fernandez for the final 10 days of the window.

Of course, the Londoners could have forced a deal through sooner but it might have meant overpaying because, as sources had previously explained, Monaco saw Camara as not for sale throughout the majority of the window - barring those few hours on Tuesday evening - but for "exceptional" offers.

Chelsea were blindsided by the collapse of the deal and there was little they could have done to revive it or sign an alternative before the deadline.

They did, however, have the option of cancelling Fernandez's move to Manchester City but opted not to do so out of a sense of "professionalism".

Chelsea wanted a midfielder to replace Fernandez but there was never any desperation as the club only wanted to do so on its own terms.

Alonso sees captain Reece James primarily as a midfield option, alongside Moises Caicedo, Romeo Lavia and new signings Jordan Henderson and Valentin Barco within his 27-man squad.

Yet injuries to Caicedo and Henderson, coupled with James' workload, meant full-back Malo Gusto was used in midfield during the 4-3 victory over Brighton, a match in which Chelsea recorded 25.6% possession, their lowest figure since records began in 2003-04.

Alonso could have selected Barco, 21, who came on as a second-half substitute, but the club want to carefully manage the signing from Strasbourg as he returns to the Premier League after a short-lived spell at Brighton.

There remains debate over whether Chelsea have sufficient depth and quality in midfield, with the club retaining the option of revisiting a move for Camara or another midfielder in January.

They could also look to strengthen other positions having been left delighted at making a net profit in the transfer market while adding quality.

Chelsea signed World Cup winner Emiliano Martinez, France international Maxence Lacroix and club-record £117m signing Morgan Rogers, as well as experienced striker Danny Welbeck and full-backs Pep Chavarria and Marco Palestra.

It's now on the manager and squad they have built to attempt to match Chelsea's ambitions on the pitch, starting with Sunday's trip to champions Arsenal.

title: Man City buy costly new midfield - but have they overlooked Haaland cover?
description: Manchester City have completed a squad overhaul including a fully revamped midfield to the tune of a Premier League record £458m, but that eyewatering number does not tell the full story.
fullText:
Manchester City have completed their squad overhaul - including a fully revamped midfield - to the tune of £458m, a new Premier League record for a summer window.

But that eyewatering sum does not tell the full story.

New Manchester City boss Enzo Maresca received the full backing of director of football Hugo Viana in his first transfer window in charge after replacing Pep Guardiola. Indeed, City's record transfer fee was twice broken this summer.

A joint-British record £125m was spent on Maresca's former Chelsea skipper Enzo Fernandez after £116m was committed on Elliot Anderson from Nottingham Forest. Morocco international Ayyoub Bouaddi, 18, was also brought in for £86m. The trio accounted for the bulk of City's summer incomings.

The departures of captain Bernardo Silva, 2024 Ballon d'Or winner Rodri, Tijjani Reijnders and Nico Gonzalez means the City midfield has been completely transformed.

Senior club sources are said to be delighted by the business done not only during the past couple of months but in January too, when plans were brought forward to sign long-term targets Antoine Semenyo and Marc Guehi.

And if the clock is rewound further back, Manchester City's rebuild of the team that won the 2023 Champions League really began in January 2025 after a difficult start to that season.

Just four players remain from the starting eleven and substitutes from the night they beat Inter Milan in Istanbul to win the continent's biggest club prize.

Maresca now has the luxury of calling upon two established players in almost every position. City feel the squad is stronger at this point than at the beginning of last season which they believe has been achieved by remaining calm and trusting the transfer strategy.

However some big questions remain.

How will their new midfield signings all fit together?

And, despite the vast amount of money spent, have they actually left themselves without a back-up to Erling Haaland?

Deadlines, acrimony and a record as Man City back Maresca for Fernandez deal

Ndiaye's journey from non-league football to £65m Man City move

City's expenditure of £542m on new signings since the turn of the year will grab the headlines, but it often goes under the radar how well they do at selling fringe players.

During this same period, they have recouped £334m, including £75m for Savinho, who scored only two Premier League goals during his time at City, as well as £65m for Rodri and £52m for Reijnders.

It gives City a net spend of £208m in 2026, which will be further bolstered by Tottenham's obligation to buy Omar Marmoush for £60m at the end of his loan spell next season.

Sources had said during the summer that they were operating on a one-out, one-in policy and Maresca managed to replace almost every player that departed, aside from Nico Gonzalez and Marmoush.

With the side well stocked at left-back, it is felt that Nico O'Reilly will play 

The club believe the record fee for Fernandez is justified by acquiring a proven winner at the highest level that will strengthen the midfield. Anderson was the summer's number one target, while 18-year-old Bouaddi is seen as having all the attributes to develop into a world class talent.

City have won back-to-back games at the start of the Premier League season and Maresca will now have a selection dilemma each game as he possesses an embarrassment of riches to choose from.

The question is how the Italian will now fit them all together.

Fernandez, Bouaddi, and Anderson are all players comfortable across multiple positions in Maresca's system.

Maresca has moved between a box and a diamond shape in midfield at City. The main difference between the two shapes is that the former has two natural holding midfielders and the second a single holding midfielder.

Against Bournemouth, Guehi paired Anderson at the base of midfield. O'Reilly, the left-sided attacking midfielder, was joined by right-back Rico Lewis, moving in-field to form the box.

Against Crystal Palace, left-back Josko Gvardiol and attacking midfielder O'Reilly flanked number 10 Rayan Cherki as the three ahead of Anderson in what looked like a diamond.

Anderson anchoring the midfield suggests Maresca sees him as Rodri's successor.

While full of praise for Bouaddi, Maresca has stressed his youth, a nod to the fact that he will likely deputise for Anderson.

Bouaddi replaced Anderson against Palace and his short cameo came soon after the introduction of Mateo Kovacic. In pre-season, the Croatian appeared to be Maresca's first choice holding midfielder but has since slid down the pecking order.

When he came on, although starting higher than Bouaddi in the midfield diamond, he dropped deep to get on the ball in holding midfield. When this happened, Bouaddi took Kovacic's position higher up.

These rotations between holding midfield and central midfield are movements Maresca may also encourage Anderson to perform when others fill the space behind him.

Versatility in the midfield four is key. Fernandez, under Maresca, was capable of playing at the base of midfield or as an attacking midfielder on both sides.

The last midfield spot, the number 10 position, has been shared between Foden and Cherki. Although Foden did play right wing against Bournemouth and Palace given City's injuries, Maresca has spoken of his central quality.

Given Foden's promising showings as a box-to-box midfielder last season – there is also a possibility both him and Cherki play through the middle together at some point this season.

Despite the positives around the recent window, Haaland is now City's only first-team striker.

The 26-year-old is pivotal to the team, ending last season as the Premier League top scorer with 27 goals, and starting the new campaign by netting twice in as many games.

But should Haaland be unavailable, what are City's options?

Marmoush wanted to play regular first-team football and was allowed to join Tottenham, while 21-year-old Divin Mubama, who did well in pre-season, joined Championship side Southampton on loan.

City believe they have enough flexibility from within their options to have not directly replaced Marmoush.

Semenyo operates mainly from the right flank but is seen as an option at number nine, having played in the position during some cup games last season.

Deadline day signing Ndiaye is another who can operate there and the £60m forward adds greater versatility and squad depth as someone who is a proven Premier League player.

However, of the forward, attacking midfield and wide options, Semenyo is the only one to get into double figures in the Premier League in the last couple of seasons.

Cherki, Jeremy Doku and Ndiaye have never hit that mark, while Foden is clearly capable, having hit 19 Premier League goals in 2023-24, but has struggled for consistent form in the last two seasons

Unless a couple of those step up, it could be one to watch if Haaland either needs to be rested or gets injured.

The Times and many companies are accusing OpenAI of misusing their material to train AI systems without compensation

The Trump administration is supporting OpenAI in ⁠a lawsuit against the New York Times, arguing in favor of the use of copyrighted writing to train artificial intelligence.

The Times accuses OpenAI and its largest financial backer, Microsoft, of using millions of newspaper articles without permission to train OpenAI’s popular chatbot. Other newspapers have joined in the suit, first filed in 2023.

In a brief filed in Manhattan federal court on Tuesday, the US government weighed in for the first time on lawsuits over the tense battle over AI and copyright. A brief has advisory rather than legal weight but could bolster tech ⁠companies as they fight the claims.

“The United States has a strong interest in continuing to develop a robust and competitive artificial intelligence industry that sets the standard for the practice and procedure of AI use globally … As such, it is critical for the United States to ‘retain global leadership in artificial intelligence’,” the brief said.

For AI chatbots to generate responses, machine learning systems are first fed billions of lines of text. The bots produce their output by statistical analysis of what the next word should be by matching a user’s query to parts of the database.

Spokespeople for the Times and OpenAI did not immediately respond ‌to requests for comment on the filing on Wednesday.

“AI dominance is critical to promote national security, prosperity, and economic mobility for all Americans,” US associate attorney general Stanley Woodward Jr said in a statement posted to X. “This Administration will never let our Nation be at a disadvantage relative to our foreign adversaries based on a plainly incorrect understanding of copyright law.”

The US commerce secretary, Howard Lutnick, separately told G20 officials ‌at a meeting in North Carolina on Wednesday that their countries should embrace fair use and allow AI companies to train their models on creators’ work while finding ​a way to “protect artists”.

All of the pending cases will probably ​revolve around whether AI systems make ​fair use of copyrighted material by ​using it to create new, transformative content. The first two judges to consider the ​question issued diverging rulings ‌last year.

The government ​agreed with ​tech companies in Tuesday’s brief that AI training is “extraordinarily” transformative.

“Beyond the subject matter of this litigation, LLMs are already helping researchers across fields achieve major breakthroughs,” the brief said. “Constraining LLM development under a misunderstanding of fair use doctrine would thwart such creative and scientific progress while hindering American prosperity and economic mobility.”
